## 5. Abandoned Reasoning

### Dead End: Treating a free tier's purpose as self-evidently "demand generation" without decomposing it

**What was tried:** Early framing assumed, as a starting point, that a free tier's job is simply to generate more paying customers (the generic PLG/demand-gen story), and proceeded to reason about volume and conversion from there.

**Why abandoned:** This begs the question (A-2). "Demand generation," "underserved-segment market coverage," "evaluation-stage competitive table stakes," and "brand/top-of-funnel discovery" are four distinct, non-equivalent mechanisms with different success metrics, different required infrastructure, and different failure modes. Treating them as one undifferentiated thing produces a plan that cannot be judged to have succeeded or failed against any specific criterion.

**What it ruled out:** A single-purpose, single-metric framing of the decision. The analysis instead carries all four candidate mechanisms forward explicitly (A-2) and tests the two most load-bearing ones directly (A-5 in chain C2, A-3/A-4 in chain C1), rather than picking one by default.

### Dead End: Parity-for-brand as an independent justification, distinct from evaluation-stage gating

**What was tried:** Considered whether "competitors having a free tier helps their top-of-funnel brand/discovery, independent of whether buyers use it to evaluate before purchasing" should be treated as a separate rival conclusion to chain C2, requiring its own separate justification and evidence path.

**Why abandoned:** Tracing the two mechanisms side by side (chain C2, hop 3) shows they imply the identical next action: this company would still need to build the same self-serve capability (GT-4?) to capture either the evaluation-stage effect or the brand/discovery effect, and would still need the same win-loss or market evidence to confirm either is actually operating. Distinguishing them in more detail does not change what this company should do next.

**What it ruled out:** Treating "which exact mechanism explains competitor parity" as a question this analysis needs to resolve before acting. It does not change chain C2's conclusion, so it was not pursued as a separate line of reasoning.

### Dead End: Using the general freemium benchmark (GT-8) as this company's expected conversion rate, rather than as a reference ceiling

**What was tried:** An early pass used the 3–5% "good" benchmark from GT-8 directly as the expected conversion rate for this company's breakeven math in chain C3.

**Why abandoned:** Chain C1 establishes that this company's self-serve activation path is untested and structurally weaker than that of the benchmarked population, most of which already has a working self-serve motion. Using the benchmark as a point estimate would have presented an untested, favorable assumption as if it were this company's expected outcome.

**What it ruled out:** Point-estimating this company's conversion rate at all. GT-8 is used only as an upper reference bracket in chain C3, with the honest conclusion being a wide plausible range rather than a single number.

### Dead End: Treating a live free tier as a cheap, easily-reversible experiment

**What was tried:** Considered modeling "launch a full free tier, and simply shut it down if the data looks bad after a quarter" as a lower-risk variant of the full-build option, on the theory that any bad outcome could be cheaply undone.

**Why abandoned:** A-10 — withdrawing free access from a live user base imposes reputational and customer-backlash costs disproportionate to those users' economic value; this is a documented pattern in freemium product management, not a hypothetical. Modeling the full build as reversible would have understated its downside-exposure score in the trade-off (chain C5) and inflated its attractiveness relative to a genuinely small pilot.

**What it ruled out:** Scoring "full build now, with an exit option" as a fourth, lower-risk option in the trade-off. It collapses into the same downside-exposure profile as "full build now" once the one-way-door property of A-10 is taken seriously.

### Dead End: Using the getmonetizely.com-sourced "15–25% of infrastructure budget" and "30–40% of support tickets" figures as verified inputs for free-tier unit cost

**What was tried:** A search for free-tier unit-cost benchmarks surfaced a vendor blog citing an unlinked "Andreessen Horowitz 2022 analysis" (15–25% of infrastructure budget spent on free users) and "Zendesk studies" (30–40% of support tickets from free users). An early draft considered using these as the basis for GT-10?.

**Why abandoned:** Neither primary source was independently located or opened by this analysis; the citing article reads as promotional content with the structural pattern of unverifiable secondary-source laundering (specific-sounding numbers attributed to named organizations with no link or reference the reader can check). Using them as ground truth would have dressed an assumption up as a verified fact.

**What it ruled out:** Presenting a false-precision cost figure. GT-10? instead carries an explicitly assumed $50–$500/account/year bracket with a Phase 3 failure record naming exactly why the stronger-looking sources were rejected.

## 6. Conclusion

**Recommended approach:** Do not build a full, permanent free tier right now. Instead, run a small, time-boxed, instrumented pilot — narrowly scoped so it cannot substitute for the paid $10,000 product — with a pre-committed kill/scale decision gate and a named owner for triaging any inbound signups it produces, specifically to measure this company's actual free-to-paid conversion rate and free-tier unit cost before committing to a full build (chain C5).

**Key insight:** The two numbers that would actually decide this question — free-to-paid conversion rate and free-tier unit cost — are both unmeasured, and the plausible range on each points in opposite directions: low assumed cost makes even weak conversion profitable, while realistic cost for a real team-collaboration product makes breakeven require performance at or above the general industry median, a bar this company's no-self-serve-history starting position gives no reason to expect it will clear (chain C3, chain C1). "Competitors already have one" does not resolve this — it is not itself a mechanism, only a fact that becomes relevant once a specific buyer-behavior claim about evaluation-stage gating is confirmed, which it is not today (chain C2).

**Trade-offs acknowledged:** A pilot delays full competitive parity and delays any upside from latent underserved demand relative to launching broadly today (chain C5); it also still carries non-zero cannibalization and sales-motion-dilution exposure relative to pure inaction, because true zero-risk scoping may not be achievable (chain C4). Running it well also requires this company to build a small amount of the self-serve/PQL-handling capability it does not have today (chain C1), which is real, if modest, organizational cost — no chain fully rules out that this cost could be higher than expected (chain C4) — no chain — flagged assumption only.

**Pre-check:** head C1 (LOW), C2 (MEDIUM), C3 (LOW), C4 (LOW), C5 (LOW) · ?-marked: none directly · lowest cited: LOW · Inputs ceiling: LOW
**Confidence:** LOW — the recommendation rests most directly on C5 (LOW), which is itself capped by C3 (LOW) and C4 (LOW); C1 (LOW) and C2 (MEDIUM) inform the supporting argument against both "parity alone justifies a build" and "the benchmark conversion rate can be assumed." This LOW rating is calibrated, not a weakness in the reasoning: it reflects that the two numbers the whole decision turns on — free-to-paid conversion rate and free-tier unit cost — are genuinely unmeasured (GT-6?, GT-10?) rather than merely unestimated, exactly as stated at the outset. What a LOW-confidence recommendation can still say with this much structure behind it is which specific action reduces that uncertainty fastest and cheapest — a scoped, instrumented pilot — and that the ranking of pilot vs. full build vs. status quo is itself robust to how the trade-off weights are set (chain C5, hop 2). The band would move to MEDIUM once a pilot produces this company's own conversion-rate and unit-cost figures in place of GT-6? and GT-10?, and the weakest-link chains (C3, C4) are two further avenues of verification named directly in those chains' confidence lines.

2	
3	*First-principles analysis · 10 October 2026*
4	
5	*Read with: [How to read this analysis](HOW-TO-READ.md) · [Working file](analysis-20261010T162514Z.md) · [All files](INDEX.md)*
6	
7	## Executive Summary
8	
9	**Recommendation:** Do not build a full, permanent free tier yet. Run a small, time-boxed, instrumented pilot — scoped so it cannot substitute for the paid $10,000 product, with a pre-committed kill/scale gate and a named signup-triage owner — to measure real conversion rate and unit cost first (chain C5).

13	**Would change it:** Real pilot data on conversion rate and unit cost (chain C3), and win-loss evidence tying lost deals to competitors' free tiers (chain C2); the pilot-vs-build-vs-status-quo ranking is itself robust to how its weights are set (chain C5).
14	
15	## 1. Problem Essence
16	
17	**Core problem:** Given that this $2.4M-ARR, 240-customer, $10,000-ACV B2B SaaS company sells exclusively through outbound sales and referrals today, has no self-serve channel at all, has never run a freemium pilot (so free-to-paid conversion is a genuine unknown, not merely an unmeasured one), and has been told by Finance that free users consume real variable infrastructure/support cost — should it build a permanently-free product tier, and if the honest answer is contingent rather than binary, what is the cheapest way to resolve that contingency before committing capital to a full build?
18	
19	**Success criteria:**
20	1. Names the specific causal mechanism(s) through which a free tier would have to create value for this company — not "competitors have one."
21	2. Produces an explicit, numeric breakeven calculation (required conversion rate / volume) anchored to the stated $10,000 ACV and the stated cost structure.
22	3. Names the organizational prerequisites this company currently lacks (per its outbound-only GTM) and what building them implies.
23	4. Treats cannibalization, sales-motion confusion, support-cost blowout, and pricing-anchor effects as explicit, quantified-where-possible risks — not hand-waved asides.
24	5. States a confidence level calibrated honestly to the stated unknowns (no internal conversion data, no self-serve infrastructure, unknown free-tier unit cost) rather than forcing false certainty.
25	6. Considers whether an option other than "build a full free tier" or "do nothing" — e.g., a scoped, instrumented pilot — outperforms the binary framing, rather than being forced to pick exactly one of "add it" / "don't add it."
26	
27	## 2. Assumptions Table
28	
29	![Assumption verdict matrix: assumption types against verdicts](report-20261010T162514Z-fig-verdicts.svg)

31	| Assumption | Type | Treatment | Verdict | Verification |
32	|------------|------|-----------|---------|--------------|
33	| A-1: "All competitors have a free tier, therefore we should add one too" (parity-as-reason) | convention | Explicitly challenge — ask what causal mechanism parity would have to operate through here before treating it as a reason | Discard — the bare parity claim names no mechanism by which it affects this company's revenue; it is not itself a reason (see chain C2) until grounded in a specific, testable buyer-behavior claim | unverified — flagged; no win-loss data cited showing deals lost to a competitor's free tier |
34	| A-2: A free tier's purpose is self-evidently the same thing every company that has one uses it for (demand-gen/PLG top-of-funnel) | untested belief | Decompose into the distinct candidate mechanisms before building: demand-gen top-of-funnel, underserved-segment market coverage, evaluation-stage table stakes, brand/word-of-mouth | Challenge — decomposed into four distinct, non-equivalent candidate mechanisms; none independently verified for this company | unverified — flagged |
35	| A-3: This product can deliver real, self-perceived value to an unassisted self-serve user with no sales-rep touch | untested belief (load-bearing) | Verify via product activation data before relying on it | Challenge — no self-serve activation data exists for this product; treated as unverified and load-bearing for conversion quality (see chain C1) | unverified — flagged; the single most consequential unverified input in this analysis |
36	| A-4: A meaningful population of prospects exists who want the product but genuinely cannot or will not pay ~$10,000/year (a real underserved segment, not just current-ICP-minus-budget) | untested belief | Verify via market sizing / lead-source analysis | Challenge — no data given on addressable long-tail demand | unverified — flagged |

182	
183	**Key insight:** The two numbers that would actually decide this question — free-to-paid conversion rate and free-tier unit cost — are both unmeasured, and the plausible range on each points in opposite directions: low assumed cost makes even weak conversion profitable, while realistic cost for a real team-collaboration product makes breakeven require performance at or above the general industry median, a bar this company's no-self-serve-history starting position (chain C1) gives no reason to expect it will clear (chain C3). 184	
185	**Trade-offs acknowledged:** A pilot delays full competitive parity and delays any upside from latent underserved demand relative to launching broadly today (chain C5); it also still carries non-zero cannibalization and sales-motion-dilution exposure relative to pure inaction, because true zero-risk scoping may not be achievable (chain C4). 187	**Confidence:** LOW — the recommendation rests most directly on C5 (LOW), which is itself capped by C3 (LOW) and C4 (LOW); C1 (LOW) and C2 (MEDIUM) inform the supporting argument against both "parity alone justifies a build" and "the benchmark conversion rate can be assumed." # Should This B2B SaaS Company Add a Free Tier

*First-principles analysis · 10 October 2026*

*Read with: [How to read this analysis](HOW-TO-READ.md) · [Working file](analysis-20261010T162514Z.md) · [All files](INDEX.md)*

## Executive Summary

**Recommendation:** Do not build a full, permanent free tier yet. Run a small, time-boxed, instrumented pilot — scoped so it cannot substitute for the paid $10,000 product, with a pre-committed kill/scale gate and a named signup-triage owner — to measure real conversion rate and unit cost first (chain C5).

**Band (from §6):** LOW (chain C5) — reflecting unmeasured inputs, not weak reasoning.

**Would change it:** Real pilot data on conversion rate and unit cost (chain C3), and win-loss evidence tying lost deals to competitors' free tiers (chain C2); the pilot-vs-build-vs-status-quo ranking is itself robust to how its weights are set (chain C5).

## 1. Problem Essence

**Core problem:** Given that this $2.4M-ARR, 240-customer, $10,000-ACV B2B SaaS company sells exclusively through outbound sales and referrals today, has no self-serve channel at all, has never run a freemium pilot (so free-to-paid conversion is a genuine unknown, not merely an unmeasured one), and has been told by Finance that free users consume real variable infrastructure/support cost — should it build a permanently-free product tier, and if the honest answer is contingent rather than binary, what is the cheapest way to resolve that contingency before committing capital to a full build?

**Success criteria:**
1. Names the specific causal mechanism(s) through which a free tier would have to create value for this company — not "competitors have one."
2. Produces an explicit, numeric breakeven calculation (required conversion rate / volume) anchored to the stated $10,000 ACV and the stated cost structure.
3. Names the organizational prerequisites this company currently lacks (per its outbound-only GTM) and what building them implies.
4. Treats cannibalization, sales-motion confusion, support-cost blowout, and pricing-anchor effects as explicit, quantified-where-possible risks — not hand-waved asides.
5. States a confidence level calibrated honestly to the stated unknowns (no internal conversion data, no self-serve infrastructure, unknown free-tier unit cost) rather than forcing false certainty.
6. Considers whether an option other than "build a full free tier" or "do nothing" — e.g., a scoped, instrumented pilot — outperforms the binary framing, rather than being forced to pick exactly one of "add it" / "don't add it."

## 2. Assumptions Table

![Assumption verdict matrix: assumption types against verdicts](report-20261010T162514Z-fig-verdicts.svg)

| Assumption | Type | Treatment | Verdict | Verification |
|------------|------|-----------|---------|--------------|

| A-4: A meaningful population of prospects exists who want the product but genuinely cannot or will not pay ~$10,000/year (a real underserved segment, not just current-ICP-minus-budget) | untested belief | Verify via market sizing / lead-source analysis | Challenge — no data given on addressable long-tail demand | unverified — flagged |

(no self-serve channel exists at all); the real requirement set also includes self-serve signup, self-serve billing/upgrade, usage metering and abuse prevention, PQL scoring/nurture, a support policy for non-paying users, and an inbound-handling adaptation of a sales org built only for outbound | unverified — flagged as an organizational gap per GT-4? |
| A-7: Free users cost the business nothing / a free tier is cost-free to run | untested belief, directly contradicted | None needed — resolved by ground truth | Discard — contradicted directly by GT-5? (Finance: costs scale with active users, not paying users) | resolved by GT-5? |

**Why abandoned:** This begs the question (A-2). Treating them as one undifferentiated thing produces a plan that cannot be judged to have succeeded or failed against any specific criterion.

**What it ruled out:** A single-purpose, single-metric framing of the decision. The analysis instead carries all four candidate mechanisms forward explicitly (A-2) and tests the two most load-bearing ones directly (A-5 in chain C2, A-3/A-4 in chain C1), rather than picking one by default.

Running it well also requires this company to build a small amount of the self-serve/PQL-handling capability it does not have today (chain C1) — the true size of that organizational cost is itself unpriced in this analysis, no chain — flagged assumption only.

Here's the first-principles breakdown.

**The real question isn't "should we add a free tier" — it's "what mechanism would make one pay off here, and are the inputs to that mechanism known?"** They're not.

**1. "Competitors have one" is not a reason by itself.** It only becomes a reason once you can show a specific causal link — e.g., buyers at evaluation stage actually choosing a competitor because of self-serve access. You have no win-loss data showing that. Your $10K team deals move through outbound sales/referrals, often with procurement review, where a competitor's free tier may be irrelevant to the actual win rate. Parity becomes a reason only after you find that evidence — not before.

**2. A free tier isn't a feature flag — it's new infrastructure you don't have.** Your GTM today is 100% outbound/referral. A real free tier requires self-serve signup, self-serve billing/upgrade, usage metering, abuse prevention, PQL scoring, and someone to triage inbound signups — none of which exists, and none of which your outbound-comp'd sales team will spontaneously own.

**3. The breakeven math is a coin flip because both inputs are unmeasured, and they point in opposite directions:**
- If free-tier cost is low (~$50/active account/year), breakeven conversion is only ~0.7% — easy.
- If cost is realistic for a real product (~$500/account/year), breakeven needs ~6.7% conversion — above the general freemium *median* (3–5%), in "great tier" territory (8–12%).
- And your starting position is *worse* than the benchmarked population: most freemium comps already had self-serve activation baked in from day one. You'd be testing self-serve activation for the first time, on a product whose activation path has only ever been sales-assisted. There's no basis to assume you land anywhere near the median, let alone the top quartile.
- At a plausible worst case (0.1% conversion), you lose money at every point in the cost range.

**4. Second-order risks a breakeven calc won't catch, and they're mostly one-way doors:**
- **Cannibalization** — a team-divisible product means some subset of a $10K team could just run on the free tier instead.
- **Pricing anchor erosion** — a permanent $0 price point gives procurement renewal/expansion leverage even among accounts that never touch the free tier.
- **Sales motion dilution** — inbound signups need an owner; diverting outbound capacity or leaving leads untriaged undermines the measurement itself.
- **Irreversibility** — shutting down a live free tier later carries backlash cost disproportionate to what those users were worth. This is not a cheap experiment you can casually unwind.

**Recommendation:** Don't build a full, permanent free tier. Run a small, time-boxed, instrumented pilot instead — scoped narrowly enough that it can't substitute for the $10K product, with a pre-committed kill/scale decision gate and a named owner for inbound signups. Its only job is to convert your two real unknowns — conversion rate and unit cost — from assumptions into measured facts before you commit real engineering and support capital.

In a weighted comparison of status quo vs. full build vs. scoped pilot (across cost-to-learn, downside exposure, preserving your existing motion, competitive-response speed, org readiness, and upside capture), the pilot wins clearly (86 vs. 48 for full build, 70 for status quo) — and that ranking holds up even if you adjust the weights significantly.

**Confidence: low, by design.** That's not a hedge — it's an accurate reflection that the two numbers this decision actually turns on are genuinely unmeasured, not just unestimated. The pilot is the cheapest way to fix that before you build anything permanent.

- If free-tier cost is low (~$50/active account/year), breakeven conversion is only ~0.7% — easy.
- If cost is realistic for a real product (~$500/account/year), breakeven needs ~6.7% conversion — above the general freemium *median* (3–5%), in "great tier" territory (8–12%).
- And your starting position is *worse* than the benchmarked population: most freemium comps already had self-serve activation baked in from day one. You'd be testing self-serve activation for the first time, on a product whose activation path has only ever been sales-assisted. There's no basis to assume you land anywhere near the median, let alone the top quartile.
- At a plausible worst case (0.1% conversion), you lose money at every point in the cost range.

**4. Second-order risks a breakeven calc won't catch, and they're mostly one-way doors:**
- **Cannibalization** — a team-divisible product means some subset of a $10K team could just run on the free tier instead.
- **Pricing anchor erosion** — a permanent $0 price point gives procurement renewal/expansion leverage even among accounts that never touch the free tier.
- **Sales motion dilution** — inbound signups need an owner; diverting outbound capacity or leaving leads untriaged undermines the measurement itself.
- **Irreversibility** — shutting down a live free tier later carries backlash cost disproportionate to what those users were worth. This is not a cheap experiment you can casually unwind.

**Recommendation:** Don't build a full, permanent free tier. Run a small, time-boxed, instrumented pilot instead — scoped narrowly enough that it can't substitute for the $10K product, with a pre-committed kill/scale decision gate and a named owner for inbound signups. Its only job is to convert your two real unknowns — conversion rate and unit cost — from assumptions into measured facts before you commit real engineering and support capital.

In a weighted comparison of status quo vs. full build vs. scoped pilot (across cost-to-learn, downside exposure, preserving your existing motion, competitive-response speed, org readiness, and upside capture), the pilot wins clearly (86 vs. 48 for full build, 70 for status quo) — and that ranking holds up even if you adjust the weights significantly.

**Confidence: low, by design.** That's not a hedge — it's an accurate reflection that the two numbers this decision actually turns on are genuinely unmeasured, not just unestimated. The pilot is the cheapest way to fix that before you build anything permanent.
